focus_profile.theme: 周三：财险、车险与巨灾风险
focus_profile.learning_goal: 关注车险定价、巨灾风险、责任险、费用率、赔付率和外部生态数据。
tasks: 选择一条财险或车险新闻，找出影响赔付频率或案均赔款的变量。
写出一个巨灾或新能源车险的风险分层思路。
记录一个可用于定价或反欺诈的数据源。

daily_concept.definition: 超过自留额后由再保险人承担约定层级损失的非比例再保险安排。

items.rss_description: Pricing at the Speed of the Market Emerging Technologies RyanMeyer Wed, 10/28/2026 - 11:33 As loss costs shift and new risks emerge, modern insurance pricing platforms are shortening the path from insight to price and changing how pricing works with underwriting. November 11, 1111 Image Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? Kumarappan Sundaram Pricing is moving from a periodic project to a continuous capability. With catastrophe volatility and shifting market conditions, treating pricing as an occasional exercise is hard to sustain. Two shifts stand out. First, dedicated pricing platforms. Rating, models and rules increasingly sit on purpose-built platforms rather than inside the core policy system. Second, modern software discipline. Version control, automated testing and continual monitoring of live models are becoming standard. Paul Carroll What is driving carriers to invest in sophisticated pricing platforms now? Kumarappan Sundaram Five things. First, speed-to-market of rate changes. Moving from quarterly or annual releases, gated by IT and policy admin deployment, to something near-continuous is the key value. Decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is also a practical starting point for core modernization, delivering value without an entire core replacement. Second, loss cost volatility and trend uncertainty. Social inflation, repair and parts costs, tariffs and secondary-peril catastrophe losses make trend assumptions go stale faster. Carriers want faster feedback from emerging claims experience that they can incorporate into price. Third, segment-level control. Carriers want to grow where they are well priced and hold the line where they are not, which means testing, deploying and monitoring changes at a granular level. Fourth, regulatory and governance demands. Filing, documentation and explainability requirements keep growing. Audit trails can be far easier to build in than to retrofit. Fifth, data ecosystem expansion. Telematics, geospatial and property-level data, cat model output and third-party enrichment should flow into rating at quote speed, which can often be the real integration challenge. A CFO will often ask how the benefit is measured, so programs should define measurement up front. Paul Carroll Underwriting and pricing are tightly linked conceptually, but loosely coupled in practice. Why is that, and can they be brought into phase? Kumarappan Sundaram The link is strong in theory but weak in practice, mainly for technology and operating-model reasons. Start with systems and data. Pricing logic sits in a rating engine or pricing platform, while underwriters work in a different workbench based on the data in the submission, so the two rarely share a view of the risk. Then there are different rhythms. Pricing changes on a release cycle, while underwriting decisions are made submission by submission. Overrides and discounts help fill the gap. Finally, the feedback loop is weak. Why underwriters override a price rarely flows back to pricing in a structured way, so a valuable signal is lost. Modern pricing platforms increasingly aim to close this gap. Bringing them into phase is mainly an integration and governance task. Pricing can be exposed as a service that the underwriting workbench calls in real time, connected to appetite, distribution, retention and claims signals. Overrides can be captured as data, and authority and guardrails can be made explicit. In complex commercial risks, underwriter judgment legitimately plays a larger role, so the aim there is visibility and learning, not automation. Paul Carroll How can modern pricing technology help carriers price emerging risks? Kumarappan Sundaram Emerging risks, such as cyber, climate-related perils and new auto and energy technologies, may not come with deep loss history. A modern platform helps in four ways. First, new data sources as proxies. Outside-in cyber scans, geospatial and property-level data, and vehicle and telematics data give carriers signals where claims history is thin. The platform brings them together with internal experience and subject matter specialist judgment, with clear rules for how the weighting shifts as claims data builds. Second, scenario testing. Teams can test prices against stress scenarios, such as a major catastrophe or a systemic cyber event. Third, fast, controlled learning. Small, measured changes show what a new risk is worth sooner and with less exposure than a book-wide change. Fourth, flexible product design. Configurable rating makes it easier to adjust deductibles, sublimits and endorsements as understanding of the risk develops. The limit can be that technology cannot create data that does not exist. For novel risks, the platform helps carriers learn and adjust quickly, alongside accumulation controls, reinsurance and underwriting oversight. Paul Carroll What impact is AI having on pricing and rating, and where should leaders be skeptical? Kumarappan Sundaram I would separate what is emerging with clear value from what is still unproven. The clearest near-term value is GenAI around the pricing process. The more underrated opportunity is in the work surrounding the price: drafting and reconciling rate filings, translating pricing specifications into platform configuration, documenting changes, summarizing competitor filings and preparing data. These steps slow the path to market, and errors are easier to review than in a pricing decision itself. What is still unproven is AI acting on pricing decisions. The idea of agents that monitor performance, propose rate actions and test them is compelling. But pricing is regulated and auditable, and many carriers are not ready for autonomous rate changes. For now, I expect AI to propose and people to approve, so the quality of that review is the real control. As AI capabilities become widely available, proprietary data, speed of deployment and governance are likely to matter more as differentiators. Carriers that treat AI as a standalone upgrade, without the platform and operating model underneath it, risk building capability they cannot put into production. Paul Carroll What would you advise a carrier to do first? Kumarappan Sundaram Measure your cycle time, from the point a pricing change is approved to the point it is live throughout the various channels. Many carriers have never seen that number, and it shows where value is being lost. Then prioritize platform and process changes that shorten it. Put governance in place before scaling AI, and start with one or two lines where faster pricing has a clear, measurable payoff. Resist modernizing everything at once. Paul Carroll Thanks. This is all super helpful. -- Kumarappan (Kumar) Sundaram is a Managing Director in PwC’s Property and Casualty Operations and Technology practice and a leader of its Insurance Core Transformation and Pricing/Rating offering. With more than two decades of consulting experience, he partners with US and UK P&C carriers, from large international insurers to small regional ones, across personal, commercial, and specialty lines, with depth in commercial and specialty. He has led numerous large-scale programs modernizing policy, claims, and pricing/rating operations, and works with PwC’s strategy, management, technology, and actuarial teams to deliver integrated solutions, thought leadership, and sales. -- Sponsored by PwC Insurance Thought Leadership ITL Partner: PwC

items.title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy

items.rss_title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.rss_description: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy PaulCarroll Mon, 11/02/2026 - 11:30 Bill Gates recently said he is using generative AI as part of the annual, two-week strategy session that determines how the Gates Foundation spends its next $10 billion. He'll be "taking the strategy notes and actually engaging in a dialogue with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and even having them talk with each other," he said. I don't have $10 billion that I'm considering how to spend, and you may not, either, but genAI has now improved to the point where it can at least be an aid in setting strategy at almost any level. An old boss, Mel Bergstein, used to say: "Strategy is what you don't do." The idea worked for Mel, who founded a consulting firm, Diamond Management & Technology Partners, that pioneered the notion of digital strategy in the mid-1990s. Chunka Mui and I took Mel's adage further in our book, "Billion Dollar Lessons," for which we had 20 researchers spend two years looking at 2,500 major failures to identify the warning signs. Our recommended solution boiled down to having a "devil's advocate" identify all the underlying assumptions for a strategy, to keep problems from being glossed over as an executive team rushed to realize the CEO's plan. GenAI, used right, can now do a pretty good job of filling that role for anyone. Let's have a look. Gates told the New York Times that, "i n a few of the reviews, we’ll actually have the A.I. sit in. In a few cases, we’ll tell it: Hey, only speak if we ask you. And then in a few other cases, we’ll say: Hey, if you hear something you think is wrong or you hear us thinking about, for example, what are these statistics? Please engage. So we’ve gone from it being a joke [when someone suggested using genAI a year ago] to it will be a peer — not making any final decisions, but it will be a peer in deep, complex strategic discussions, making a significant contribution." I'm not willing to go that far just yet, partly because I'd need to test the domain knowledge that the large language models have about a subtle, heavily regulated business like insurance and partly because genAI has shown itself to be a sycophant. The biggest, overarching pattern of failure that Chunka and I found in the research for " Billion Dollar Lessons " was that people were reluctant to point out obvious problems that could derail initiatives that had the imprimatur of the CEO, and we don't want to replace human sycophants with AI ones. But you can describe your strategy to an AI, then pepper it with questions, going deeper each time while demanding evidence for its thinking and insisting it be blunt. Let's say you're thinking of buying a company. You could start with a general question: What could go wrong? Then you probe. How will our competitors react? What if interest rates increase? The economy goes into recession? The war in Iran escalates? Will we actually be able to cross-sell to our customers? Will the efficiencies from scale be as great as we expect? Who's done something similar and had problems? What were the problems? And on and on and on. You can do the same exercise if you're thinking of a new line of business, a software overhaul, adopting AI chatbots — or if you want to explore the dangers of standing pat, of not undertaking a major initiative that is under consideration. Major corporations have staff do extensive analysis along the lines I'm suggesting and, in the case of a possible acquisition, draw on their investment banks for advice — but the bias is always toward acting. If the perception is that the CEO backs an idea, the staff strives to make it work, not to kill it. Investment banks only collect their hefty fees if the deal happens, so why would they recommend against it? When Chunka and I did a consulting project with a major company that was considering launching autonomous vehicles, we saw elaborate studies it had commissioned from consulting firms that said the robotaxi business was a slam dunk and that the first to enter would win big. That was more than eight years ago. It turned out, however, that the executives working on the AV project internally were aware of all the sorts of operational and safety issues that we've all seen play out and that have slowed the robotaxi rollout. Those concerns were brought to the surface in the interviews for our devil's advocate review. Warren Buffett used to set aside two, equal pots of money when asking investment banks for advice on possible acquisitions — one for a bank that argued in favor of a deal and one for a bank that argued against it. Whichever carried the day collected its fees, while the other got nothing. You can be sure the "anti" bank worked as hard as possible on its arguments and evidence. In my experience, many big ideas should fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. As we wrote in "Billion Dollar Lessons," we thought 47% of the failures we investigated were based on strategies that never should have made it out of the strategy room — and not because those involved were stupid or inexperienced. The fifth-biggest cement maker in the world reasoned that it was really in the home products business because so much of its cement was used there. It began also making furnaces and lawn mowers... then went bankrupt and was bought by a competitor. Avon decided that its core competency was its culture of caring — not, you know, its line of cosmetics and its devoted salesforce — so it bought a maker of medical equipment and an operator of retirement homes. It had no idea how to operate the new businesses and quickly sold them at a major loss. In the early days of fax machines, FedEx spent hundreds of millions of dollars to set up a business that would collect a document from you, drive it to the nearest office, fax it to the office nearest your destination, then drive the fax to the recipient. The company somehow missed that Moore's law would soon make the devices so inexpensive that every company would have its own. It may take time to learn how to use genAI to avoid costly strategic mistakes — and that's even before we start using it as broadly as Gates is planning to. You'll likely also need to introduce to the LLM information specific to your market, including regulatory issues that it likely doesn't have even as these models try to Hoover up everything available on the internet. Insurance is a complicated market. But I think we're now at the point where genAI can, if managed correctly, start to catch strategic errors. We won't get that 47% figure for obviously bad ideas down to zero, but even heading toward 40%, maybe even 33%, would mark real progress. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll At any level of setting strategy, from the boardroom to the one-person agency, generative AI can bring assumptions to the surface, helping you see what NOT to do. items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? items.summary: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? Read More How AI Can Transform Submissions for Underwriting by Prathap Gokul Commercial insurers face a strategic challenge: identifying which submissions merit scarce underwriting attention, not just processing more faster. items.rss_description: Go Beyond the Flow Leadership ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/28/2026 - 09:32 Workflow platforms boost efficiency, but synchronous interaction builds the social capital that makes digital collaboration truly effective. Excerpted from "Social Capital at Work." November 3, 2026 Image Collaboration. It's what every leader hopes for in her team. It's the purpose behind much of our communication at work. And it can be a challenge. There is a collaboration platform in the digital workplace for almost everything. Salesforce. Asana. HubSpot. Figma. Git. ServiceNow. Too many to name them all. Each tracks and assigns work items and enables us to collaborate through a system. The systems sit between us. They enable us to tell one another what to do online. Want something done, open a ticket. Want to feel productive, pound through your task list, and assign "work items" to the next person in the workflow. Fire, then forget. Most of the time, this works just fine. The efficiency can't be disputed. But ask yourself a couple of questions. Are there times you assign a task in Salesforce and get back a result you didn't expect? Have you ever opened an Asana task and not known what you were being asked to do? Our experience tells us it happens all the time. Communication scholars and system architects make a distinction between synchronous and asynchronous messages. Synchronous communications occur in real time and involve immediate back and forth between participants. Asynchronous communications allow for time delays. Workflow assignments are asynchronous. They happen independent of an immediate response. Sometimes, in fact, responses don't happen at all. Workflow makes it easy to make an ask of a colleague, assign a task to a subordinate, offer feedback to a collaborator. They also eliminate the synchronicity of a person-to-person "handoff." Evidence suggests synchronous interaction makes us feel connected at work. It even fosters relationships, which make asynchronous communication on workflow platforms more effective. An intriguing study of software engineers proves it. The engineers worked in two buildings several blocks apart. In some instances, teams worked together in the same building. In others, the team members were spread across the locations. As is common in the software industry, the engineers used a platform to share code, give one another assignments, and provide feedback. Researchers found that teams of engineers working in the same building—that is, colleagues who had frequent synchronous interactions with one another—received 23% more online feedback—an asynchronous interaction—on their code than did those on multi-building teams whose members had less frequent face-to-face contact with one another. "Sitting near workers increases not only in-person but also digital collaboration," the authors write. The collocated software engineers enjoyed the benefits of social capital: mentorship, coaching, learning, and collaboration. All were achieved through a digital tool that, when coupled with the opportunity for synchronous interaction, worked for and not against social capital. Everyone benefited, especially those newest to the team. Retention among newer joiners was significantly higher among collocated teams than dispersed teams. Young workers and women, the authors tell us, are "substantially more likely to quit the firm when they lose proximity to coworkers." Less feedback. Less connection. Lesser results. It's a lesson the system architects at Amwins, led by Ben Sloop, took to heart when they designed their collaboration platform. Ben knows his way around a spreadsheet. A boardroom, too. Harvard undergrad. Stanford MBA. A stint as a management consultant at Bain, then a few years in private equity. The perfect pedigree for his current role as president and chief operating officer of Amwins, the nation's largest wholesale insurance broker. But there's more to Ben's success than his stellar resume. Ben told us, "One of the core requirements to gain more responsibility here is having deep, real relationships with our salespeople. I spend a disproportionate amount of my time talking to and staying connected with people in the field. Of all the people that I'll respond to, first is if one of our brokers reaches out to me. That's the top of my inbox." Amwins' clients are retail insurance brokers and agents looking to find homes for complex, hard-to-place risks—think workers' compensation insurance for circus performers. The insurance carriers who advertise on the Super Bowl don't want the hard stuff. And so, retail brokers work with wholesalers like Amwins to get complex risks placed with one of a large legion of specialty insurance carriers. Each occupies a well-defined niche within the commercial insurance market. Each is expert in a particular type of risk. This creates a classic many-to-many problem. Thousands of customers, thousands of carriers and thousands of Amwins brokers sitting between them. The challenge is having the right expertise at the right time. "Our brokers have to be specialists," Ben told us. "Our retailers don't want to work with someone that does everything a little bit, because that's kind of what they do. They want to deal with someone that's a deep expert." Enabling his brokers to always find that one expert within their large, decentralized organization became a key part of Amwins' founding mission. It's the hardest part of what they do, Ben told us. "In order to be a deep expert, what that means is that, well, if my client comes to me and they ask me for a construction wrap policy in Scottsdale that I know nothing about, I've got to know where to get them what they need inside our own firm. So, we don't lose that client, right? And so, this created this huge coordination problem." The company built Amlink to solve it. Amlink is the wholesaler's proprietary relationship management system. It is a workflow platform, but it's different. Ben beamed with a creator's pride as he told us how it works. "I can look in the system and say, well, actually, we have a guy who lives in Scottsdale and does only construction wraps, right? And so, I can reach out to that person who I usually know personally, because we have all sorts of sales events. The point is to build connectivity with an internal coordination mechanism." We both have seen lots of systems that tried to solve similar problems. All did it the same way. Type in "construction wrap in Scottsdale" and you'd get deal listings, PowerPoint presentations, maybe a white paper or two. Lots of stuff to wade through, maybe some good slides you can reuse, but probably not the answer you need. Amlink is different. It delivers names and contact information and forces conversations to happen. It's effective at both delivering expertise when it's needed and building relationships across the firm. Knowing who to turn to can make or break a deal. Amwins brokers don't just compete on expertise—they compete on connectedness. Amlink is a unicorn. "I've never seen another system in the industry like this. Everyone says it's a people business. but they tend not to track [data] at the people level," Ben told us. He was clear to put the tech in its proper context: "We are a technology-enabled business. The thoughtful use of technology makes our people better. But we are fundamentally a person-to-person business." Social capital matters at Amwins. It drives market results. It also creates an environment where people want to stay. "You know, it's funny. I joined 19 years ago, and I still think of myself as one of the newer people," Ben confessed, explaining that Amwins was the kind of place "good people stay for a long time. People typically don't leave just for money. People tend to leave because they just don't feel connected, don't like who they're working with, don't feel compelled by the strategy." We probably should have introduced you to Ben at the very beginning. " Social Capital at Work ," by John Burrows and Seth Rachlin, will be published by Simon Acumen on Nov. 10. This article is excerpted from their book. John Burrows Seth Rachlin

items.rss_description: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/26/2026 - 17:11 Bill Gross recently announced a free database of AI-generated ideas for innovative companies, based on the 31 methodologies that he's developed over the past three decades and that have powered his Idealab incubator. The list of ideas — currently totaling a whopping 1,208,580 — may or may not contain an idea that you'll be able to turn into big bucks, but I think that exploring the database and interacting with the ideas is worth a bit of your time. Many of the notions I see for the insurance market are provocative. They can at least suggest where there are holes in insurance offerings today that you should work to fill, even if you don't launch the sort of standalone company that Gross would love to see join his pioneering incubator. Let's have a look. Here is a link to the database . And here is a link to a Fortune article that describes the effort in detail, including Gross's argument that innovations driven by AI will create far more jobs than it will eliminate. The article says Gross's prompts to the AI break down into three categories: "O pportunities, which he says are things such as solving a business pain point, removing friction, removing waste, removing danger, and improving design, among others; enablers, such as new technologies, scientific advances, and new materials, processes, or changing cost curves that make solutions more feasible than before; and shifts, such as regulatory changes, as well as behavioral, economic, cultural, or geopolitical movements that make the timing for a particular business seem right. " Gross also fed his AI " some 17 million source documents that included news stories, research reports, expired patents, public company filings, and threads from online community discussion boards" and came up with his 1.2 million ideas for new businesses. But are the ideas any good? I certainly found them thought-provoking. For instance, I selected the "fintech/insurtech" option, specified that I didn't want to invest more than $250,000, wanted to get to market within a year and hoped to "make the insurance claims process smoother for customers." The top suggestion, which the AI suggested was a 57% fit for me, was for a "claims trust operating system that... gives policyholders visibility into the evidence shaping settlements and repairs." I'm not sure that's a business. It would take an awful lot of work to assemble the huge amount of settlement and repair data that would be needed to be truly definitive, but the idea raises an intriguing notion: Somebody will surely try to use an AI to give policyholders a quick handle on what the insurer will likely offer after a car accident, water damage to a home, etc. If the insurance industry provides the initial take, it will be able to lower expectations and control payments. If plaintiff attorneys fill the need, they'll be able to raise expectations, influencing policyholders to be disappointed... and perhaps hire an attorney to contest the offer. The competing interests would seem to create an opportunity for a trusted intermediary, but I, at least, have become skeptical about whether it could stay unbiased. I subscribe to the notion laid out by Cory Doctorow in a seminal blog post republished by Wired magazine in 2023 that describes the process of — excuse my French — enshittification. As I wrote at the time , Amazon is a great example. It initially built a huge base of customers by doing everything possible to make life simple for them. Once it had the customer base, it courted businesses — and the customer experience started to get gunked up by ads, attempts to keep customers from easily finding the best deals, etc. Once Amazon had built a marketplace where companies had to have a presence, it started milking them as much as possible on behalf of investors — a fee here, a fee there, maybe Amazon would even use its insights into sales data to launch products or businesses that would undercut a company with a hit offering on Amazon's platform. (Amazon has consistently denied doing so but has faced many lawsuits alleging it does.) Just about everybody still uses Amazon, but the experience is very different than it was a decade ago. Even if I'm right that there isn't a business in a "claims trust operating system," the Idealab database has still pointed to a sore spot that the insurance industry needs to address. Somebody is going to use AI to shape policyholders' thinking about what to expect as a settlement, by providing near-instant estimates. So insurers should at least be thinking about how they show their work, and quickly, to keep plaintiff attorneys from setting unrealistic expectations and accelerating the trend toward more and more litigation. So I'd recommend that, whatever your role in the insurance ecosystem, you poke around in the database to see what friction points and opportunities it has surfaced that you might be able to address. There are more ideas than I can count about underwriting, pricing, services from agents and brokers, and on and on. If you're like me, your eyes glaze over after half an hour or so of an exercise like this, so maybe make a visit to the database an occasional excursion over the next month, perhaps at the end of the day as you're winding down or before a weekly meeting with colleagues so you can stir up discussions. We all get locked into our mindsets and into our day-to-day routines, and Gross has provided a whole host of prompts that can challenge us to do ever more than we are now. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The founder of Idealab has used AI to generate more than 1.2 million ideas for innovative AI-based companies, including in insurance. They're thought-provoking. items.extracted_text: SafePoint secures its largest catastrophe bond ever, $650m Nature Coast Re 2026-2 - Artemis.bm SafePoint secures its largest catastrophe bond ever, $650m Nature Coast Re 2026-2 - Artemis.bm SafePoint secures its largest catastrophe bond ever, $650m Nature Coast Re 2026-2 4th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard SafePoint Insurance Company has successfully secured its largest catastrophe bond yet, as the Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) issuance has been priced to provide a 160% upsized $650 million of collateralized reinsurance protection, while the company also managed to get the coverage at a pricing level below initial guidance, Artemis has learned. SafePoint made its return to the catastrophe bond market in October. Initially, the target was to secure a $250 million source of multi-year named storm reinsurance protection . However, as we reported in our first update on this transaction, SafePoint was targeting a meaningful upsizing for the deal, more than doubling it to provide up to $600 million of multi-year reinsurance protection, while at the same time, the price guidance for both tranches of notes on offer had been lowered too. Earlier this week, we learnt that SafePoint had raised the target size again for its latest catastrophe bond sponsorship, to $650 million, while the price guidance for the two tranches of notes had been revised again at the low-ends of the updated lower ranges. We’ve now been informed from sources that the notes have been successfully priced to secure the 160% upsized $650 million of multi-year named storm reinsurance protection. Now priced, this Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) issuance marks the largest catastrophe bond that SafePoint Insurance Company has ever sponsored. This also marks the sixth cat bond under the Nature Coast Re special purpose insurer, and SafePoint’s tenth cat bond sponsorship overall. You can read all about SafePoint’s cat bonds in our extensive Artemis Deal Directory . We won’t repeat all the details of this new cat bond in our updates on size and pricing, so make sure to visit the Deal Directory entry to learn more background on the transaction . Special purpose insurer (SPI) Nature Coast Re will now issue two tranches of Series 2026-2 catastrophe bond notes to source reinsurance for SafePoint Insurance Company itself and the two reciprocal exchanges it operates. The notes are designed to cover losses from named storms on an indemnity and per-occurrence trigger basis, while the reinsurance protection will run across a four-year period from December 1st. As we’ve previously explained, this Nature Coast Re Series 2026-2 issuance will cover losses in the widest range of US states of any cat bond in SafePoint’s history, supporting the insurer’s continued expansion and growth into new locations. What was initially a $100 million tranche of Series 2026-2 Class AA notes were then increased to $300 million, which is where the offering was finalised. The Class AA notes come with an initial base expected loss of 0.73% and were first offered to cat bond investors with price guidance in a range for a spread of between 4% and 4.75%, which was first lowered to between 3.75% and 4%, and were then eventually fixed at the lowest-end of 3.75%. What was initially a $150 million tranche of Series 2026-2 Class A notes were first increased to $300 million, before they increased again to $350 million in size terms, which is where the offering was finalised, we are told. The Class A notes have an initial base expected loss of 1.66% and were initially offered to cat bond investors with price guidance in a range for a spread of between 6.75% to 7.5%, which was then lowered to a revised range of 6.25% to 6.75% and were then offered with a spread of 6.25%, which is where the notes eventually priced, so again at the low-end of the updated range. This is a great result for SafePoint, as the company has managed to capitalise on investor appetite within the catastrophe bond market, in being able to secure meaningfully more reinsurance than initially sought, while also securing the coverage at attractive pricing. It’s important to note that SafePoint also has another cat bond sponsorship in the works. As we reported earlier this week, SafePoint is looking to secure $100 million of annual aggregate and industry-loss index triggered named storm protection through an Arthur Re Ltd. – Nature Coast Re 2026-3 catastrophe bond offering, that will provide retro reinsurance to the company’s captive reinsurer. As a reminder, you can read all about this new Nature Coast Re Ltd. (Series 2026-2) catastrophe bond and the Arthur Re Ltd. – Nature Coast Re 2026-3 issuance, as well as every cat bond deal ever issued in our extensive Artemis Deal Directory . All of our Artemis Live insurance-linked securities (ILS), catastrophe bonds and reinsurance video content and video interviews can be accessed online. Our Artemis Live podcast can be subscribed to using the typical podcast services providers, including Apple, Google, Spotify and more. items.extracted_text: Axor Financial launched as $1bn insurance capital platform by Cohen. Hires Fox from HCMA - Artemis.bm Axor Financial launched as $1bn insurance capital platform by Cohen. Hires Fox from HCMA - Artemis.bm Axor Financial launched as $1bn insurance capital platform by Cohen. Hires Fox from HCMA 4th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Axor Financial has been launched with a vision to provide the right capital into the insurance and reinsurance industry, with the new business that has been founded by former Gallatin Point exec Zhak Cohen recognising the need for alignment between capital providers and the industry participants they are funding. Axor Financial explains itself as, “A $1 billion principal capital platform dedicated to insurance — marrying flexible, long-term capital with insurance focus and expertise.” Founder Zhak Cohen has a wealth of experience investing in and deploying a wide-range of capital solutions to the insurance and reinsurance markets. Cohen spent almost nine years working at sector-specialist investment firm Gallatin Point Capital LLC, during which time he became a Managing Director and Member of the Investment Committee and allocated capital across a wide-range of opportunities in the re/insurance sector. His work has included hybrid capital platform builds in the insurance industry, transformations of company capital architecture, formations of NewCo’s and alternative capital investments. He previously worked in the alternative reinsurance capital division at XL Group. In his time at Gallatin Point, the firm also became a catastrophe bond sponsor with the Marlon Re issuance in 2024. Cohen also spoke at one of our conferences in New York in 2025, where he explained accessing the cat bond market was a way to marry Gallatin’s risk appetite with those of other investors . When he launched Axor Financial Cohen explained, “The premise is simple: insurance does not lack capital it lacks the right capital—capital of the appropriate form and quality, committed for the right duration, available at meaningful scale, and backed by a deep understanding of the businesses and risks it supports. “Axor was created to help close that gap by providing flexible, long-term capital and strategic solutions across the insurance industry.” The goal at the new company is to provide flexible, long-term capital solutions at institutional scale to insurance and reinsurance industry participants. This can include everything from equity, through hybrids, surplus relief solutions and structured risk capital solutions, so insurance-linked securities type financings and arrangements are likely in scope. Importantly, Axor Financial wants to work with investors and capital providers that match the needs of the re/insurance market. In having the right form, quality, risk appetite and duration, while being available in sufficient scale, to truly deliver solutions that match the way the re/insurance industry plans and works. Axor Financial brings an understanding of the various market constituents that require access to financing, with the investor connections to support those needs and a goal to align both sides “so everyone is underwriting the same outcome.” This week, Axor Financial has announced its first hire as well, with former Howden Capital Markets & Advisory (HCMA) Director Tim Fox having joined as a Principal. Fox had worked at HCMA, the capital markets focused arm of reinsurance broker Howden Re, since June 2016, focusing on U.S. M&A, capital raising and reciprocal formation transactions. Cohen commented on the first addition to his new venture, “Tim Fox has joined Axor Financial as a Principal — our first full-time hire — and I couldn’t be more excited. “I’ve known and worked with Tim for nearly a decade as he rose through the ranks at Howden’s investment banking division. He’s bright, humble, hardworking and technically proficient, with the integrity and judgment you want in a colleague. “Axor’s thesis is simple: the insurance industry doesn’t lack capital it needs the right capital — flexible, long-duration, institutional in scale, and backed by deep, dedicated insurance expertise. That thesis is resonating, and we’re off to a stronger start than I could have hoped. “Building on that momentum comes down to people, and I can’t think of a better first hire.” To be clear, Axor Financial is not an ILS business, but it is the latest specialist to launch with a mandate to deploy capital to financing solutions in the industry, which will likely over-time include some participation in risk-linked structures, as well as equity, debt and other hybrid financing forms. With institutional third-party capital increasingly focused on developing efficient ways to access the returns of the re/insurance sector and new capital deployment routes emerging, while industry participants are increasingly sophisticated in how they leverage external sources of financing, Cohen’s timing may be opportune. items.extracted_text: Alternative capital driving greater options for insurance buyers: Aon - Artemis.bm Alternative capital driving greater options for insurance buyers: Aon - Artemis.bm Alternative capital driving greater options for insurance buyers: Aon 4th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard The expansion of alternative and institutional capital alongside traditional reinsurance is helping expand program choice for insurance buyers, according to broker Aon’s Q3 2026 Global Insurance Market Insights report. In its report, the broker underlines that abundant capacity, and strong insurer competition continues to support favourable conditions for buyers across most major lines and geographies. However, the broker states that what is fundamentally changing is the nature of the capital supporting the market, along with the risks demanding its attention. According to Aon, strong reinsurer balance sheets and favourable treaty renewals are being supplemented by committed, multi-year institutional and alternative capital, giving clients more options to structure their insurance programs and access capacity. “Capital is changing shape, and that matters more than the headline pricing numbers. Strong reinsurer balance sheets and favorable treaty renewals have supported capacity this year. Alongside that, we have seen steady growth in committed, multi-year capital from institutional and alternative sources, sitting directly alongside the traditional market. This diversification creates a deeper and more stable capital base – one that is more resilient to future shifts in market conditions,” Aon’s report reads. “For clients, the practical effect is choice: more sources of capacity and more ways to structure a program than were available even a few years ago. It is also reshaping the conversation at the underwriting table. As more capital competes for well-managed risks, clients with strong data and a clear narrative can be more deliberate about who they partner with, and on what terms.” The broker emphasises that the choice extends heavily beyond traditional insurance, with clients increasingly turning toward captives, structured solutions, parametric products and other alternative risk transfer options for extra flexibility. At the same time, these solutions can also help organisations manage volatility and align risk financing more closely with their broader business goals. While catastrophe activity has been relatively benign in 2026, which has helped to contain claims volatility and also contributed to softer property market conditions. Aon’s report cautions that lower losses do not mean underlying exposures have diminished. The broker also highlights that digital infrastructure and AI are creating new risk considerations. This shouldn’t be too surprising given the on-going data centre expansion, which is increasing demand for insurance capacity across construction, commissioning and operations. As we’ve said in previous articles, the global data centre build-out is heavily pushing traditional insurance capacity to its limits, which in turn presents a key opportunity for the capital markets. Earlier this year, Swiss Re Institute indicated that AI data centres and renewable energy infrastructure alone could generate around $200 billion in insurance premiums between 2026 and 2030, who also outlined how this opportunity creates a clear role for alternative reinsurance capital, particularly in regards to catastrophe bonds and sidecars. Furthermore, Aon’s report also highlights how the property insurance market has continued to soften throughout 2026, driven by abundant capacity, favourable reinsurance conditions and intensifying competition among insurers for quality risks. “Well-performing, well-managed risks across the U.S., UK, Latin America and Pacific markets have achieved double-digit pricing reductions, with even greater reductions in India. Competition is extending beyond price, with insurers seeking greater participation and lead positions while offering increased limits, broader coverage and more flexible terms,” Aon said. “The underlying market dynamics reflect strong reinsurer balance sheets, favorable reinsurance renewals and continued appetite from both traditional and alternative capital providers, enabling insurers to deploy additional capacity across most industries. However, the market remains highly differentiated by risk quality. Loss- impacted and natural catastrophe-exposed risks and higher-hazard occupancies continue to face greater underwriting scrutiny and more measured pricing relief, although increased capacity is improving options even for some challenging risks.” Importantly, Aon’s report underscores that regional conditions remain heavily inconsistent across the property market. Japan continues to face increasing pricing pressure, whereas the rate reductions in China has slowed down as insurers focus more on profitability due to recent regulatory adjustments. In general, the market has transitioned from a state of limited capacity to one of competitive capacity, with the most significant benefits going to risks that can showcase strong loss performance, effective risk management, and a reliable dedication to risk improvement. Christian Hoffman, CEO of Commercial Risk, Aon, commented: “Favorable market conditions give clients an opportunity to strengthen their risk programs, not simply reduce cost.” Hoffman added: “Clients can use better exposure data to test limits and retentions and consider where savings can be reinvested to build greater resilience. Strong data and a clear understanding of risk remain critical to achieving the best outcomes. items.extracted_text: New APCIA Initiative Looks to Help ‘Backbone’ of Industry With Regulatory Costs Article 0 Comments Small and midsize carriers “form the backbone” of the private insurance market, and they are being bogged down by the cost of regulatory and corporate compliance. The American Property Casualty Insurance Association (APCIA) is starting an initiative to try and do something about that. David Bell, chair of the APCIA and CEO of an insurer in the small to medium category – ALPS Corp., said a recent study by the APCIA found that “these companies bear disproportionately higher compliance costs relative to premium than larger insurers.” “The study also found that scale materially affects compliance impacts on the expense ratios,” Bell said recently at APCIA’s annual meeting in Boston. “A fixed regulatory cost does not have a fixed impact between large and small carriers.” Related: APCIA Says Claims Data Standards in Works to Better Combat Criticism Eight out of 10 members of the APCIA have less than $2 billion in direct written premiums. And while they may not have nationally well-known names or move financial markets at earnings time, they “insure farms, professionals, small businesses, homes, and communities across the country,” Bell said. “Collectively they give our private competitive marketplace much of the depth, specialization and resilience that it enjoys.” However, discussions with 20 small and medium carriers on APCIA’s board confirmed there is a need to reduce regulatory costs that are amounting to what Bell described as a “scale tax” that is paid “not because the company presents more risk, but because it has fewer premium dollars across which to spread a largely fixed cost.” “Delays in approvals, filings or licensing, costly and inconsistently applied state exam formats – they don’t just cost money, they cost opportunity,” Bell said, adding that when the admitted market becomes slower, capital and product innovation migrate to the excess and surplus lines market – a “structural rather than situation” migration. APCIA’s proposed Small and Medium Sized Insurer Regulatory Cost Initiative (SMSIRCI) will work to pursue regulatory improvements and benefits for carriers that will hopefully trickle to consumers once changes positively affect the expense ratios of small and medium-sized carriers. (Bell acknowledged the initiative’s less-than-catchy acronym. “It sounds more like a wifi router password than it does an insurance initiative. So the first act of regulatory simplification will be simplifying the name.”) Bell said he expects policymaker scrutiny as some historical norms are challenged, but he believes the initiative can include cooperation with state regulators to pursue improvements that benefit consumers while maintaining a competitive insurance marketplace. items.extracted_text: Insurance Technology Firm Paperclip Acquires Apis Productions Article 0 Comments Paperclip, Inc., a New Jersey-based insurance technology company, announced that it has completed the acquisition of Apis Productions, LLC. Apis provides technology for the insurance industry including websites and portals, hosting and security, custom application development, marketing, and AI consulting services. Formerly operated as Apis Productions in Annapolis, Maryland, the business now operates as Apis Technologies, a wholly owned subsidiary of Paperclip. Paperclip is focused on secure data exchange, document intelligence, workflow, and orchestration services. Terms of the transaction were not disclosed. “The acquisition of Apis represents an important step in Paperclip’s evolution into a broader, connected insurance technology platform,” said Ron Alexander, chief executive officer of Paperclip. He said the acquisition strengthens Paperclip’s ability to connect insurance carriers, distributors including wholesale brokerage general agencies and independent marketing organization, producers, and other providers through more seamless digital experiences and technology-enabled services. Paperclip said it will continue supporting existing Apis customers. Peri Lane, founder and current CEO of Apis Productions, will continue to lead the day-to-day operations of Apis Technologies as its president. items.extracted_text: Municipal Insurer Must Pay Share of $14.9 Million Wrongful Incarceration Settlement Article 0 Comments A Massachusetts Superior Court judge recently found a municipal insurer responsible for a share of a $14.9 million settlement with a man wrongly incarcerated for 36 years. MIIA Property & Casualty Group, Inc. was ordered to pay the town of Braintree 40.62%, or $6,052,380, of the $14.9 million settlement in a law enforcement liability case. MIIA insures cities, towns and government entities in the Commonwealth against property/casualty losses. As one of the town’s insurers, MIlA provided Braintree with law enforcement liability and general liability coverage for the years 2002-2017. The percentage of MIIA’s share of the settlement reflects MIAA’s “time-on-the risk,” with other insurers picking up the earlier years. Suffolk Superior Court Judge Peter B. Krupp in Boston found that MIIA was liable under the law enforcement liability policy but not the general liability coverage. For 36 years, Fredrick Weichel was incarcerated for a 1980 murder in Braintree that he did not commit. After his release, Weichel sued the town and some of its employees. After settling those suits for $14.9 million, the town sued MIIA for refusing to indemnify it for part of the settlement. Weichel’s 1981 conviction was overturned in 2017 after it was learned that the Braintree police department had a report and evidence identifying another man as the murderer but the police never informed defense counsel, state police or the district attorney of that report. It was only after Weichel’s attorney made public records requests in 2010 and 2013 that the report was released. The Superior Court ultimately granted Weichel a new trial, finding that the report was plainly exculpatory and contradicted the Commonwealth’s theory of Weichel’s involvement in the murder. Weichel’s conviction was overturned and he was released, having served approximately 36 years of a life sentence. After his release he sued the town in the federal district court for Massachusetts in Boston, asserting claims for violations of his constitutional rights and for malicious prosecution, as well as claims for bodily injuries while in prison and mental and physical health problems that continued even after release. He also alleged that between 1980 and 2009, the town withheld the exculpatory report despite multiple records requests and rearranged documents in the report’s binder to sow confusion about the evidence, delaying his release by at least four years. In connection with the federal litigation, MIlA engaged a law firm to represent the town and paid the town’s defense costs. At the same time. MIIA reserved the right to deny indemnification with respect to a judgment or settlement paid to Weichel. In December 2020, Weichel offered to settle for $36 million. About two years later, in a civil suit against the Commonwealth, a Suffolk Superior Court jury found Weichel actually innocent and awarded him $33 million, which was reduced to the $1 million statutory cap. The following January, defense counsel advised MIIA that the town potentially faced “astronomical damages” and recommended attempting to settle the case, while noting that it would be difficult to settle because of the $33 million verdict rendered against the Commonwealth. Weichel reduced his demand to $22 million and then to $14.9 million, but he refused to lower the demand further. In September 2024, the town agreed to pay $14.9 million to settle the litigation. Braintree proposed that MIlA and its other insurers contribute pro rata based on each insurer’s time-on-the risk and subject to each insurer’s liability limit. MIIA believed that it had no indemnity obligation for any portion of the Weichel settlement, never offered more than $1 million, and rejected the use of a pro rata allocation. The town entered into the $14.9 million settlement without MIlA’s agreement to participate. The town then sued MIAA alleging the insurer breached its duty to indemnify and engaged in unfair claim settlement practices in violation of the state’s consumer protection statute for failing to pay its share. The parties moved for summary judgment. The judge allowed the town’s motion for summary judgment on the duty to indemnify claim but granted MIAA’s motion to dismiss the unfair claims practices claim. Judge Krupp reasoned that because the underlying litigation settled, the court must look to “the basis for the settlement” to determine an insurer’s indemnification obligation, and the “relevant inquiry” is “how the parties to the settlement viewed the relative merits of the plaintiff’s claims at the time of the settlement.” He found that the town satisfied the burden of demonstrating that the claimed acts that formed the basis for the settlement were covered by a MIIA policy. The town argued that by settling with Weichel, it compensated him for bodily injury that occurred during his imprisonment that fell under the law enforcement liability policy. MIIA contended that the town did not show that the occurrence of imprisonment caused bodily injury, or that bodily injury occurred during its contract period (2002-2017). The judge sided with the town, noting that under the plain language of the insurance contract, Weichel’s wrongful imprisonment was a continuing “occurrence” arising from the town’s law enforcement activities. He referenced the record at settlement that indicated bodily injuries after 2002 including undertreated infections (2002-03), injury from inmate assaults (2006-07), open wound left unaddressed for over a year (2011), and basal cell carcinoma untreated for a year (2016-17). The judge also noted that prior to mediation, Braintree and MIIA considered literature regarding injuries arising from long-term incarcerațion. Moreover, the Suffolk Superior Court jury awarded Weichel damages after evaluating “physical pain and suffering, and mental pain and suffering.” The judge concluded that the basis for the town’s settlement of federal claims included Weichel’s claim for bodily injuries that occurred within the coverage period. The town had met its burden to show a duty to indemnify on this basis. The town also argued that the post-conviction failure to produce the exculpatory report and the improper production of the report in 2010 fell within the MIIA contract period. MIIA argued that the offense of wrongful conviction and false imprisonment occurred at the time of conviction, and that the post-conviction failure to produce the report did not create an additional injury or trigger coverage. MIIA further argued that Weichel’s claim of improper production of the report was “far- fetched” and Braintree had not given it credence. The judge noted that under Massachusetts law, an initial wrongful conviction does not trigger coverage during the entire imprisonment period. However, the judge continued, failure to disclose exculpatory evidence in response to record requests may constitute a separate offense that would trigger a duty to indemnify under MIIA’s policies. The relevant inquiry thus is “how the parties to the settlement viewed the relative merits of the plaintiff’s claims at the time of the settlement.” Before the settlement, MIlA recognized in a letter to National Casualty Co. that Weichel’s allegation of a failure to produce the exculpatory report would trigger personal injury coverage in years in which requests were ignored. The town also showed that the allegation was not considered meritless at the time. The town also believed that Weichel would be a credible and sympathetic witness to the jury. Citing these undisputed facts, the judge found that Braintree had demonstrated that the settlement was partially based on alleged post-conviction offenses of failure to respond to record requests, which triggered MIlA’s indemnification obligation. MIIA also argued that there was no coverage due to an exclusion in the law enforcement liability policies that was triggered because the town knew about Weichel’s false imprisonment prior to its contract period. But the judge found that MIlA failed to prove the town or its police officers knew of the injury before the contract period. Topics Carriers Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: Cyberattackers Drain Money From French Bank Credit Mutuel Arkea Article 0 Comments Crédit Mutuel Arkéa said hackers stole money from it after gaining access to its computer systems, underscoring the growing cybersecurity risks for the banking sector. The French lender “was the victim of a cyberattack that enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out,” a spokesperson confirmed to Bloomberg News on Wednesday, declining to say how much money was stolen. The spokesperson said some transactions have been suspended and the bank is in contact with authorities about the attack. The situation is “under control” and there won’t be a financial hit to clients. Related: Binance Hackers Used Fake Job Interviews in $6.3 Billion Heist It’s the latest example of cyberattacks on banks around the world. The State Bank of India, the country’s largest lender by assets, recently launched a probe after a suspected cyberattack exposed thousands of customer records containing personal information. In Japan, a wave of data breaches has hit companies including Daiwa Securities Group Inc., East Japan Railway Co. and SoftBank Corp., prompting government officials to step up cybersecurity measures. Hackers also recently pulled of the biggest heist that the digital-asset industry has ever faced, draining more than $6 billion from crypto exchange Binance. Cyber risks are increasing “exponentially” and represent “the price to be paid for all this innovation,” UBS Group AG Chief Executive Officer Sergio Ermotti said earlier this week. Good governance, clear accountability and the ability to react quickly in this environment are key, he added. Crédit Mutuel Arkéa earlier this year filed an application to obtain a MiCA authorization, the European regulation on crypto-assets, to offer crypto services to its customers. items.extracted_text: EFAMA says cat bonds a "precious diversifier", UCITS eligibility should remain unchanged - Artemis.bm EFAMA says cat bonds a "precious diversifier", UCITS eligibility should remain unchanged - Artemis.bm EFAMA says cat bonds a “precious diversifier”, UCITS eligibility should remain unchanged 4th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans The European Fund and Asset Management Association (EFAMA) has urged European Union policymakers to leave the status of catastrophe bonds unchanged in the UCITS Eligible Assets Directive (EAD), calling the asset class a “precious diversifier” and saying that “limiting asset choice within UCITS per se is not in investors’ best interest.” EFAMA, a trade association that represents the EUR 33 trillion European investment management industry, has issued a paper in response to the European Securities and Markets Authority’s (ESMA) technical advice regarding cat bond eligibility under the UCITS investment framework. Recall that, ESMA made a recommendation in June 2025 to the European Commission, not to allow catastrophe bonds as eligible assets in UCITS funds, a move that has generated wide-attention across the insurance-linked securities (ILS) industry. EFAMA highlights that under ESMA’s proposed approach catastrophe bonds may only be eligible within the 10% limit for alternative assets, within a UCITS strategy. But EFAMA calls for policymakers to consider the important role of catastrophe bonds within portfolio diversification and natural disaster risk transfer, highlighting that the asset class deserves to have its eligibility status unchanged. Federico Cupelli, EFAMA’s Deputy Director of Regulatory Policy, commented, “Catastrophe bonds offer investors relevant diversification benefits and have a well-established secondary market. Rather than revisiting their eligibility, policymakers should focus on preserving the conditions that have enabled such instruments to contribute effectively to UCITS portfolio construction. The current UCITS EAD framework is effective and should remain in place.” Dan Irwin-Brown, EFAMA’s Director of Market Insights, Data & Analytics, added, “Cat bonds offer valuable diversification benefits because they are exposed to insurance-related risks whose drivers differ from those influencing traditional financial assets. They are a good example of why investors should retain access to alternative asset classes within the well-regulated UCITS framework.” UCITS catastrophe bond funds hit a combined nearly $21.8 billion in assets under management at the end of September 2026 , demonstrating how important this fund structure has become for the ILS investment sector. EFAMA notes that UCITS cat bond funds are an important and growing component of the catastrophe bond market, a marketplace that delivers meaningful benefits to its investor base in the portfolio diversification it offers to them, as well as to society in the vital disaster risk transfer the capital supports globally. The trade association stated, “With regards to the EAD review, EFAMA is of the opinion that any reform should maintain the credibility and recognition of the UCITS label globally. It believes UCITS should retain a degree of flexibility to access – in a controlled manner – the benefits of limited exposure to assets uncorrelated to financial markets. It also believes investors should have access to an investment portfolio that reflects contemporary best practices in allocation and diversification terms, allowing asset managers to access the broadest possible investment universe while enabling the UCITS brand to play its part in the climate change transition and adaptation efforts.” The EFAMA paper highlights “the advantages of keeping less traditional asset classes in UCITS portfolios,” using catastrophe bonds as an example. It drives home the message that cat bonds are a “precious diversifier” for investors, with ESMA’s own analysis showing correlations of just 0.19–0.29 with major asset classes they examined. In addition, cat bonds have an active secondary market and their liquidity compares well to other asset classes, with EFAMA saying, “estimated annual secondary-market turnover is 23%, versus 33% for investment-grade and 19% for high-yield European corporate bonds.” In addition, industry estimates suggest that direct retail investors make up just roughly 1% of the UCITS cat bond investor base, while UCITS access is also important for allocators whose mandates restrict other fund structures. In fact, access to UCITS cat bond funds is largely through institutional, professional, and intermediated channels, with banks and wholesale investors, wealth managers and independent financial advisers, pension funds, fund of funds and family offices making up the remainder of allocations to this investment segment, EFAMA notes. With the insurance protection gap still significant around the world, the ability of the capital markets to contribute vital risk capital through instruments such as cat bonds is also seen as socially important, when it comes to natural disaster risk transfer. Regarding potential changes to the UCITS Eligible Assets Directive (EAD) that might be considered, EFAMA urges that “any reform should maintain the credibility and recognition of the UCITS label globally.” UCITS strategies should retain a degree of flexibility, in a controlled manner, to provide the benefits of exposure to asset classes that are uncorrelated to financial markets, the paper explains. EFAMA concludes in its paper that, “Any review of the UCITS EAD should not lead to material changes affecting investors interested in the wrapper, which would likely require the USD 21bn within Cat bond-focused UCITS to be adjusted through reallocation, conversion / relaunch into another structure, or potentially fund closure. “Many alternative assets – as illustrated with a specific asset class in this Market Insight – exhibit low correlation to traditional assets. Cat bond drawdowns have historically been less severe on a portfolio level than historic drawdowns in equity markets. They therefore act as a precious diversifier. Combining all alternative exposures into a 10% threshold, as currently proposed, would strongly limit investor diversification and return benefits. “In the case specifically of UCITS Cat bonds, aside from the benefits for investors (primarily diversification), there are also important benefits to society (i.e. filling the insurance protection gap) as well as sponsors (i.e. allowing them to free capacity for further insurance needs), which should be taken into account when considering the potential stifling of the market from the demand side.” EFAMA also explains that, “Absent evidence of significant market failure / investor harm from the current eligibility interpretations, limiting asset choice within UCITS per se is not in investors’ best interest, esp. by eliminating controlled exposures to alternative assets beyond the mere 10% ‘non-eligible’ limit. “Finally, an established market – in this case that of Cat bonds – can mobilise capital rapidly and at scale. Further restrictions on UCITS investment in Cat bonds could disrupt the existing investor base, as affected investors would need time to find alternative investment structures or might no longer be able to participate, potentially reducing the market’s capacity to mobilise capital when it is needed most.” There has been no response from the European policymakers to ESMA’s technical advice so far, but the topic remains high on the agenda within the asset management community and EFAMA now adds its voice to the calls for any response to be prudent and to consider the benefits that assets such as catastrophe bonds provide to investors, the sponsors of the instruments and to wider society. You can read the full paper via the EFAMA website .
